use: A close, fast orbit about 500 km up. You see fine detail and a lap takes about 95 minutes, but a ground station sees you only briefly each pass.

mechanics.note: Low Earth orbit period check; simplified two-body model.

use: A tilted orbit that passes over each place at the same local time every day. Lighting stays the same, so pictures can be compared over months and years. Landsat uses it.

mechanics.note: This period check does not calculate the J2-driven nodal precession required for a true sun-synchronous orbit.

use: An orbit so high that one lap takes 24 hours, the same as Earth’s spin. The spacecraft stays above one spot, so it can watch the weather there all the time.

mechanics.note: The reference uses one sidereal day. Station-keeping and longitude control are not modelled.

use: A low orbit over the Moon’s poles. As the Moon turns below, the spacecraft sees every part of it. It loses contact when it goes behind the Moon.
d: Hidden behind the Moon at times.

mechanics.note: Circular lunar-polar destination orbit. The Earth-to-Moon transfer leg is not propagated in this game.

use: A Sun-centred, highly elliptical trajectory. Parker Solar Probe repeatedly approaches the Sun, reaching a perihelion of about 6.1 million km. The exact orbit changes over the mission.

mechanics.note: Perihelion is supplied, but semi-major axis or aphelion is not. A complete Kepler period cannot be derived from perihelion alone.
